tldr: A Diffusion Policy trained solely on indoor handheld demonstrations successfully transferred to a real-world aerial manipulator outdoors without retraining, thanks to onboard LiDAR odometry and whole-body MPC with zero reliance on external motion-capture infrastructure.

overview:
Aerial manipulators—drones equipped with robotic arms—hold great promise for inspection and maintenance in high or hazardous locations. However, outdoor operation faces steep hurdles. The aerial platform wobbles every time the arm moves. Outdoor environments also lack high-precision indoor motion-capture systems, while exposing the system to wind disturbances and lighting variations.

To overcome these challenges, the authors proposed an integrated framework combining end-effector-centric imitation learning, whole-body Model Predictive Control (MPC), and precise onboard LiDAR state estimation. For imitation learning, they adopted a Diffusion Policy well-suited for smooth trajectory generation, trained on just 80 demonstrations collected indoors using a handheld device.

In validation experiments, an outdoor peg-in-hole task was performed on an open lawn, inserting a 20 mm diameter peg into a 50 mm hole while hovering. No external cameras, GNSS corrections, or outdoor retraining were used. The platform maintained an indoor-comparable normalized tracking error of around 0.1 m and platform tilts under 4 degrees, achieving successful insertion across all trials. This work marks an important step toward bringing learning-based aerial manipulation out of the lab and into the wild.
contributions: Building a complete real-world outdoor aerial manipulation framework integrating Diffusion Policy, onboard LiDAR-inertial odometry (FAST-LIO2), and nonlinear whole-body MPC.
Formulating a lightweight whole-body MPC that coordinates the floating base and multi-joint manipulator in real time to follow learned end-effector trajectories.
Demonstrating physical real-world generalization to an unseen outdoor task using only handheld demonstrations gathered indoors, without additional outdoor demonstrations or retraining.

sections.heading: Background: Taking Lab-Bound Aerial Manipulators into the Wild
sections.summary: Aerial manipulators offer immense value outdoors, but most prior learning-based methods have relied on motion-capture-equipped indoor spaces. This work investigates whether a visuomotor policy trained entirely on indoor demonstrations can transfer directly outdoors using only onboard sensors.
sections.details:
Conventional unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have achieved remarkable results in passive sensing tasks such as infrastructure inspection and aerial cinematography. Taking this a step further, aerial manipulation attaches arms or end-effectors to actively exert physical contact with the environment. However, moving an arm on a floating aerial base induces reactive forces that perturb platform attitude, making it exceptionally hard to reconcile flight stability with millimeter-level end-effector positioning.

Recently, imitation learning that learns control directly from human demonstrations—particularly Diffusion Policy with its superior temporal consistency—has shown impressive gains in robot manipulation. Mobile and aerial manipulation researchers have begun adopting it, yet most efforts remain confined to indoor settings. Venturing outdoors forfeits millimeter-wave or optical motion capture (MoCap) systems, while introducing visual shifts from sunlight and physical disturbances like wind gusts.

Historically, outdoor aerial manipulators have relied on hand-engineered, task-specific perception and control pipelines. Such designs, however, cannot answer the fundamental question: can dexterous behaviors learned from demonstrations transfer across diverse environments? This paper aims to demonstrate that a policy trained strictly on indoor end-effector demonstrations can be deployed directly outdoors via onboard sensors and whole-body MPC, without any retraining.

sections.heading: System and Architecture: Decoupling End-Effector Policy from Base Dynamics
sections.summary: The system pairs a fully actuated hexarotor with a 4-DOF arm. A Diffusion Policy trained on handheld data generates relative end-effector trajectories, which an onboard LiDAR odometry system and real-time whole-body MPC translate into coordinated platform-arm motions.
sections.details:
### II-A System Overview
The experimental platform consists of a fully actuated hexarotor with tilted rotors, a 4-DOF serial manipulator, and an OAK-1W camera mounted at the end-effector. Demonstrations are gathered using a handheld "UMI device" that mirrors the real arm's camera and gripper configuration. This enables efficient demonstration collection by hand without having to fly the real drone repeatedly.

### II-B End-Effector-Centric Diffusion Policy
The visuomotor policy adopts a Diffusion Policy (DDIM sampling) that stochastically predicts future action sequences from observation histories. The key element is an end-effector-centric representation. Network inputs are the end-effector camera's RGB images, relative end-effector poses, and gripper widths. The outputs are future trajectories of end-effector relative positions $\mathbf{p}^{\text{ee}}$, relative orientations $\mathbf{R}^{\text{ee}}$, and gripper width commands $w$.

Confining the policy to the end-effector space completely decouples it from platform-specific dynamics like rotor thrusts and joint angles. Moreover, operating in relative end-effector coordinates rather than global coordinates prevents over-reliance on absolute world-frame positioning accuracy, ensuring robustness.

### II-C Whole-Body Model Predictive Control (Whole-Body MPC)
To track the predicted end-effector trajectories, a nonlinear MPC jointly optimizes the platform base and manipulator. The state vector comprises base position, velocity, Euler angles, angular velocities, and arm joint angles. To enable high-speed real-time optimization, the controller uses a lightweight dynamic model with small-tilt approximations for the base and a first-order lag model for the closed-loop joint controllers.

The MPC objective minimizes end-effector position and orientation tracking errors while enforcing costs that keep the base nearly level (minimizing roll and pitch) and regularize the arm near a nominal posture $\mathbf{q}_0$. This nonlinear optimization problem is solved using acados with the SQP-RTI (real-time iteration) scheme, applying only the first computed control input to the platform and arm to achieve smooth, stable whole-body coordinated motion.

sections.heading: Hardware Experiments: Indoor-Trained Policy Operates Outdoors in the Breeze
sections.summary: The setup was evaluated on inserting a 20 mm peg into a hole 130 cm above the ground. Using a model trained on 80 indoor demonstrations and state estimation from onboard LiDAR (FAST-LIO2) alone, all 5 indoor and 3 outdoor trials succeeded without human intervention.
sections.details:
### III-A Experimental Setup
The team chose a challenging peg-in-hole task: inserting a 20 mm diameter peg held by the drone into a 50 mm hole mounted 130 cm off the ground. The training set consists of only 80 indoor demonstrations collected via the handheld device. Domain randomization was applied by shifting initial and target positions to teach diverse approach trajectories. For outdoor tests, no external motion capture was used; state estimation relied solely on the onboard LiDAR-inertial odometry system, FAST-LIO2.

### III-B Indoor and Outdoor Experimental Results
First, five baseline trials were conducted indoors. Across varying initial and target poses, all five trials succeeded. The normalized end-effector tracking error remained at 0.102, with the whole-body MPC smoothly coordinating the base and arm toward the target.

Next, the platform was brought to an unseen outdoor lawn area and tested directly, without any additional learning or fine-tuning. Despite harsh conditions—harsh sunlight, different backgrounds, and wind disturbances—all three outdoor trials achieved autonomous insertion from takeoff without human intervention.

Comparing indoor and outdoor performance, the normalized end-effector tracking errors were on par, confirming that switching from external MoCap to onboard LiDAR did not degrade accuracy. Furthermore, maximum platform tilt (roll and pitch) stayed below 4 degrees across all environments, providing quantitative proof that the whole-body MPC maintained platform stability while precisely guiding the end-effector.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Outlook: Bridging the Gap from Lab to Real World
sections.summary: Integrating an end-effector Diffusion Policy, onboard LiDAR odometry, and whole-body MPC enables outdoor aerial manipulation directly from indoor demonstrations without retraining. Future work points toward more diverse tasks and harsher outdoor conditions.
sections.details:
This study presented an outdoor-capable aerial manipulation framework that ties together Diffusion Policy imitation learning, onboard LiDAR-inertial state estimation, and whole-body MPC.

Hardware validation proved that a policy trained on a small set of indoor handheld demonstrations can zero-shot transfer directly to an unseen outdoor environment without external motion capture or outdoor retraining. Decoupling an end-effector-space policy from a model-based whole-body controller proved highly effective at balancing environmental robustness with flight stability.

For future directions, the authors plan to evaluate the framework on more diverse, complex manipulation tasks beyond peg-in-hole, as well as test disturbance rejection under adverse weather conditions such as stronger winds.

takeaways: Decoupling end-effector imitation learning from coordinated base-arm execution (whole-body MPC) abstracts away complex drone dynamics, vastly boosting policy transferability.
Using a relative end-effector coordinate frame and egocentric vision minimizes the impact of background shifts and global positioning errors between indoor training and outdoor deployment.
Pairing high-precision onboard LiDAR-inertial odometry (FAST-LIO2) with fast nonlinear MPC (acados) enables millimeter-to-centimeter aerial manipulation outdoors without external MoCap.
limitations: Evaluation is limited to a single rigid peg-in-hole task; extension to contact force feedback or deformable object manipulation has not yet been demonstrated.
Outdoor testing comprised only three trials; evaluating robustness under harsher conditions, such as strong winds, rain, or feature-sparse open fields for LiDAR, remains future work.
